steps.title: What this step is for
steps.text:
One molecule crossing the spot does not always leave one burst. It wanders out and back, and the burst search — which sees only a count rate — cuts the passage into two or three bursts.

This tool merges those fragments back into one burst and writes a new burst folder. Nothing in the folder you start from is changed, so you can try a threshold, look at it, and throw it away.

Start by choosing the burst folder burst selection produced — the one holding bi4_bur.

steps.title: Step 1 — see the evidence before choosing anything
steps.text:
Press Run now, with the settings as they are.

Nothing is written. It reads the burst tables and estimates P(same molecule) against the lag between bursts: the probability that a burst arriving τ after another one is the same molecule recurring, rather than a different molecule arriving by chance.

Watch the first plot. It starts near 1 at short lags — a burst 100 µs after another one is almost certainly the same molecule — and falls as the lag grows.

steps.title: Step 2 — read your threshold off that curve
steps.text:
The dashed line is this number. The dotted line is the longest lag at which the curve still meets it — the gap that will actually be fused.

Try 0.9 and press Run again, then 0.3. The dotted line moves, the burst count in the summary moves with it, and the histograms change shape.

There is no universally right value. High is conservative (only obvious splits are repaired); low eventually merges genuinely different molecules. The plot is there so the trade-off is yours to see.

steps.title: Step 3 — the ceiling that is not about probability
steps.text:
Now look at where the dotted line sits relative to the curve. On a dilute sample the curve stays above any sensible threshold out to tens of milliseconds — the molecule really is the same one, because there is hardly anyone else in the sample.

Fusing on that would be correct about the molecule and ruinous for the burst. A burst on disk is one interval, so bridging a 70 ms gap puts 70 ms of background inside the burst.

That is what this box stops. The probability answers 'same molecule?'; this answers 'at what cost?'. Leave it at 10 ms unless you know why not.

steps.title: Step 4 — what fusing did to your bursts
steps.text:
Read the summary table before writing anything. The rows that matter:

• Bursts — how many single-molecule events you now have.
• Proximity ratio (std) — should fall. A fragment has fewer photons than the passage, so its ratio is shot-noise-broadened; repairing the split narrows the distribution.
• Photons per burst — should rise, and the photon histogram should lose weight from its short tail.
• Duration (mean) — rises too, because the bridged gaps are inside the burst now. If it jumps by orders of magnitude, your ceiling is too generous.

steps.title: Step 5 — write the fused folder
steps.text:
Press Save.

This is the slow half: the photon streams are reopened and every column of the new burst table is re-derived over the real span, so the fused folder is a burst folder in every respect — BVA, 2CDE, the MLE and H2MM read it with no idea that fusion happened.

The plots then switch from the preview to what was actually written (the legend says so). The two differ by the background the bridged gaps brought in; the fu4 companion records that number per burst.

steps.title: Step 6 — and then carry on down the pipeline
steps.text:
The later steps now point at the fused folder.

One thing to know: companions already computed on the original folder — BVA, 2CDE, per-burst MLE lifetimes — are not carried over. They have one row per original burst and would misalign against the fused ones. Recompute them here, which is exactly why fusion sits before them.

If you decide against it, simply go back a step: the original folder was never touched.
